title: Finally! The World's Fairest Dice — and It Took 15 Years!
summary:
Have you ever argued with your friends about who goes first in a board game? Well, some mathematicians just solved that problem — with dice that have 60 sides each! And it took them 15 years to figure out.

It all started at a gaming convention around 2010. A board game designer named James Ernest asked his friend Eric Harshbarger a tricky question: Could you make a set of dice so that no matter how many people play, everyone has an equal chance to go first? No ties, no rerolls.

Harshbarger, a mathematician at Auburn University in Alabama, didn't know the answer that night. But the question stuck with him. For the next 15 years, he and his friends worked on it. Finally, they cracked it!

The answer is five dice, each with 60 sides. Together, they have every number from 1 to 300, with no repeats. If you roll them, the person with the highest number goes first — and it's perfectly fair for any group, from 2 to 5 players.

Why was it so hard? "The easy thing is to avoid ties; you just put different numbers on all the dice," Harshbarger said. "The problem comes in how you distribute those different numbers across the dice so that the probability is equal not only for the whole set but for any subset."

That means if three people play, they can grab any three dice and still have fair odds. Same for four or five players.

The team even discovered their dice do something extra cool: they can determine the whole turn order, not just who goes first. Every possible order is equally likely!

To celebrate, Harshbarger built giant wooden copies of the dice, each from a different type of wood. They're on display at Auburn University's new math building.

So next time you can't decide who goes first, maybe you'll get to roll a 60-sided die. Just don't lose it under the couch!
why_it_matters: Fairness questions pop up in everyday life, like deciding who goes first, and this story shows that math can help solve them.

Most dice have six sides, but some special dice have many more sides.
These five new dice are special because no matter which ones you pick, every player has a fair chance.
Article_Structure: WHO: James Ernest asked the question; Eric Harshbarger and mathematician friends worked out the answer.
WHAT: They made five 60-sided dice that fairly choose the first player for any group of 2 to 5 players.
WHERE: The idea began at a gaming convention around 2010, and the wooden dice are now at Auburn University in Alabama.
WHY: Because ordinary dice can cause ties, and earlier designs were not fair when players used only some of the dice.

perspectives.description: They get a set of dice that ends tie arguments and gives every player a fair shot.
They solved a puzzle that took 15 years and showed that a hard fairness problem in probability can be cracked.
They might still use simple dice or apps at home, since 60-sided dice are more special than everyday games.
